But only to create instability.

I've been holding on to this video for several years now, to attach to a note in my journals about left and right (which I still haven't had the chance to finish).

Although the concepts of left and right are inadequate and vague for capturing the complexities of today's global political landscape, they can still be somewhat useful for conveying and understanding messages.

In this video, Bezmenov, a KGB associate and insider, explains that using leftists is useful—"but only up to the point of creating instability in countries."

The interview was recorded in 1984.

Link

Let me emphasize once again: if you ask my opinion, for our country today we want neither left nor right. What we want is a different way of looking at things—one that aligns with the left on some positions and with the right on others.

Almost the opposite of most of those segments that have today been adopted from—or have ended up aligning with—the conventional left and right in our political structure.

Strategy at the Individual Level

You've heard me say this a lot, but since I brought up resource constraints, I'd like to repeat it once more:

Whenever someone tells me, "Starting today, I want to do such-and-such" (study a language, read books, exercise, ...),

my first question to them is:

"What are you going to stop doing starting today?" Because your day wasn't 23.5 hours before, that you'd now want to add half an hour to it. Until yesterday you also had 24 hours, and now you want to add a quarter hour or half an hour of a new activity to it. So something has to give.

Now either you're going to watch fewer movies,
or go to fewer parties,
or sleep less,
or exercise less,
or check Instagram and Telegram less,
or ...

If someone hasn't clearly answered this second question, that first thing they said is just a passing fad. Sooner or later, you should expect them to rattle off all sorts of excuses for "it not working out" and "giving up."

Strategy hurts (1)

Following my previous point about the vision, it's worth adding a few more notes. I've said these things many times over the years. But repeating them is useful too. They're worth constantly repeating and hearing.

My friends.

Strategy is always and always accompanied by resource allocation. The resources at our disposal (money, time, connections, etc.) are limited, and strategy is supposed to help us allocate these limited resources better.

"Resource allocation" is different from "resource distribution."

Resource distribution means I spread whatever I have across different tasks, different resources, different departments, and try to make sure everyone gets a piece.

Resource allocation is a scientific and precise term with a specific meaning.

Resource allocation means we think about who we want to give these limited resources to (and who we don't).

By defining, formulating, and executing strategy, we always create dissatisfied people. If you see that a strategy meeting was held, everyone sat together and talked, and at the end everyone came out smiling, know that the only thing wasted in there was the sugar and tea and the fruit of the meeting.

Must, must, must, some people come out of the strategy meeting upset. These are the same managers, the same departments, and the same projects that have been allocated fewer resources.

"A collection of all good things" is not a strategy

Yesterday I watched the conversation between Mr. Abdeh Tabrizi and Mr. Mohammad Fazeli.

I hold both of these dear gentlemen in respect, and the points Mr. Abdeh Tabrizi made about macroeconomics were certainly instructive for me and all his students (as they always have been).

But at one point in the conversation, Mr. Abdeh Tabrizi said about the 20-year Vision Document: "We drafted this document in 1384, when Ahmadinejad had not yet come to power, and the document's goals seemed achievable."

Linking the failure to realize the Vision Document to Ahmadinejad's coming to power (which certainly dealt a great blow to national interests) does not seem logical to me.

The Vision Document was a completely wrong document from the very beginning. It was a beautifully written essay that had no strategic nature (while an upstream document of this kind should naturally have a strategic nature).

This document was "a collection of all good and attractive things." Strategy is not of this kind. Strategy means letting go of many good things and setting priorities among other good things, and specifying which good thing we are willing to sacrifice for the sake of another good thing.

If these questions are not answered in a document, that document is nothing more than an essay.

I consider it one of my honors that from those very years, when I was teaching strategy, I taught this document as an example of a completely wrong document, and I told my students that this document is not a vision—it is merely eye-catching.

That document was wrong on the first day too; with Ahmadinejad or without Ahmadinejad, for Iran or for Saudi Arabia or for America.

It was a beautiful essay that seemed poetic and attractive. But my judgment is that anyone with even a little literacy in strategy would never have been willing to sign beneath that essay.

#Maybe_Temporary
